key_terms.meaning: Building a picture on screen from a numerical model stored in the computer.
Starting from a picture already captured and changing it to extract or improve information.
One picture element — the smallest addressable colour cell in a raster grid.
Image stored as colour values on a fixed grid of pixels; zooming in shows the grid.
Image stored as shape descriptions (lines, curves, fills); the renderer draws the grid at output time.
Number of addressable pixels across and down the display, written as width × height.
Width of a pixel or frame divided by its height; 4:3 and 16:9 are common frame ratios.
Number of bits used per pixel; 8 bits gives 256 levels per colour channel.
The block of memory holding one full frame of pixel colour values for the display.
Beam sweeps every scan line left to right, top to bottom, refreshing all pixels each frame.
Beam draws only the line segments held in the display list, in any order.
Number of times per second the picture is redrawn, in hertz (Hz).
Colour made by adding red, green and blue light; (0,0,0) is black, (1,1,1) is white.
Colour made by subtracting cyan, magenta and yellow ink from white paper; C = 1 − R, M = 1 − G, Y = 1 − B.
Same colours re-described as hue angle (0°–360°), saturation (0–1) and value/brightness (0–1).
A state-machine graphics API: settings persist until changed, and vertices pass through a fixed pipeline.
Digital Differential Analyser: steps along the longer axis by 1 and adds a float increment to the other axis.
Chooses the next pixel with one integer decision variable updated by addition only.
Uses one decision variable per step to pick between two candidate pixels, then mirrors into eight octants.
Deciding which pixels a geometric shape covers and setting their colour values.
A run of neighbouring pixels on one scan line lying inside the polygon.
Fill that spreads from a seed pixel to all 4- or 8-connected neighbours of the same colour.
Sampling picks pixel positions from a continuous scene; quantisation rounds each value to a finite set of levels.
Jagged edges or false patterns caused by sampling a continuous image at too coarse a grid.

takeaways: Computer graphics starts from a model and makes a picture; image processing starts from a picture and makes numbers.
A raster stores colour at every grid point, so its size in memory is width × height × bits per pixel.
A vector file stores shapes, so it stays sharp at any output resolution but needs a renderer to become pixels.
Raster scan displays refresh the whole screen line by line; random scan displays redraw only the lines in the display list.
RGB adds light for screens, CMY subtracts ink for print, and HSV is RGB rearranged so a human can pick a colour.
OpenGL is a state machine: you set state once, then send vertices and the pipeline produces coloured fragments.
DDA is simple but uses floating point; Bresenham reaches the same pixels with integer additions only.
The midpoint circle algorithm needs only one decision variable per step and eight-way symmetry to finish a circle.
Scan-line polygon fill uses an edge table and an active edge table to fill whole spans instead of testing every pixel.
A digital image is a sampled, quantised scene, and the eye judges quality by contrast and edges rather than by exact pixel values.
bank_note: Long answers here usually mix a definition-plus-comparison part with a worked numerical trace — expect to draw a table of pixel positions or an edge table, not just describe the algorithm in words.

bank.q: Distinguish computer graphics from image processing. Give two applications of each and explain what the input and output are in each case.
outline: Graphics: input is a numerical/geometric model, output is an image
Image processing: input is a captured image, output is a modified image or measurements
Graphics examples: CAD part design, cricket broadcast overlays, metro maps, game scenes
Image processing examples: medical scan enhancement, weather radar map cleanup, photo filters
Both meet in a pipeline — images are used as textures inside graphics, and graphics images are processed afterwards

bank.q: Compare raster graphics and vector graphics. Define pixel, resolution, aspect ratio and bit depth, and state the memory needed for a 1024 × 768 raster at 24 bits per pixel.
outline: Raster: colour stored per grid cell; fixed resolution; zoom shows blocks
Vector: shapes and coordinates stored; renderer produces pixels at output size
Pixel = smallest addressable picture element
Resolution = width × height in pixels; aspect ratio = width/height
Bit depth = bits per pixel; 24 bits gives 16.7 million colours
Trade-off: raster is simple and fast to display, vector scales cleanly

bank.q: Explain raster scan and random scan display systems with block diagrams. Cover the display processor, frame buffer, display list and refresh.
outline: Raster scan: beam sweeps each scan line in order, whole frame stored in frame buffer
Refresh rate in Hz, e.g. 60 Hz means 60 complete frames per second
Display processor converts drawing commands into frame-buffer writes
Random scan (calligraphic): beam draws only segments in the display list, no frame buffer of pixels
Random scan gives smooth lines and no aliasing but cannot fill areas easily
Comparison: memory, filling ability, line quality, cost

bank.q: Explain the RGB, CMY and HSV colour models. Give the conversion relations between RGB and CMY, and explain why HSV is preferred for colour picking.
outline: RGB: additive, used for screens; axes R, G, B each 0–1
CMY: subtractive, used for ink; C = 1 − R, M = 1 − G, Y = 1 − B
K (black) added in CMYK to save ink and get true black
HSV: hue as angle 0°–360°, saturation 0–1, value 0–1
V = max(R,G,B); S = (max − min)/max; hue from which channel is the maximum
HSV separates colour from brightness, so a slider for hue stays intuitive for a user

bank.q: Describe OpenGL as a state machine and list the stages a vertex passes through in the graphics pipeline.
outline: State machine: current colour, matrix, lighting persist until changed
Vertex data supplied with glVertex or vertex buffers
Vertex processing: model-view and projection transforms
Primitive assembly and clipping
Rasterisation into fragments with interpolated attributes
Fragment processing: texture, colour, depth test
Framebuffer output; swap buffers to show the frame

bank.q: Use the DDA algorithm to rasterise the line from (2, 3) to (9, 7). Show the table of x, y and rounded pixel positions for every step.
outline: dx = 7, dy = 4, so steps = max(7,4) = 7
x increment = 7/7 = 1, y increment = 4/7 ≈ 0.571
Table of (x, y, rounded y) for steps 0 to 7
Show that one pixel is plotted per x column because x is the longer axis
Note the rounding rule used (round to nearest integer)

bank.q: Rasterise the line from (1, 1) to (8, 5) using Bresenham's line algorithm. Show the initial decision parameter and its update at every step.
outline: dx = 7, dy = 4, initial p₀ = 2dy − dx = 1
If p < 0 choose E and p = p + 2dy; else choose NE and p = p + 2dy − 2dx
Step-by-step table of p, chosen pixel and updated p
All arithmetic is integer, no division inside the loop
Final list of plotted pixels from (1,1) to (8,5)

bank.q: Generate the first-quadrant pixels of a circle of radius 8 centred at the origin using the midpoint circle algorithm. Show the initial decision parameter and list the mirrored points.
outline: Start at (0, r) = (0, 8), initial p₀ = 1 − r = −7
If p < 0 pick E and p = p + 2x + 3; else pick SE and p = p + 2x − 2y + 5
Table of x, y, p for each step until x ≥ y
Plot eight symmetric points (±x, ±y) and (±y, ±x)
Total plotted points = 8 per computed point

bank.q: Explain the scan-line polygon fill algorithm. Build the edge table and trace the active edge table for two consecutive scan lines of your chosen polygon.
outline: Edge table: buckets by smallest y, each entry stores ymax, x at ymin and slope 1/m
Active edge table holds edges crossing the current scan line, kept sorted by x
Fill between pairs of intersections (even-odd rule)
On moving to next scan line, add new edges and update x by adding 1/m
Remove edges whose ymax is reached
Span coherence: fill a whole run of pixels at once, no per-pixel inside test

bank.q: A pixel has RGB value (0.2, 0.6, 0.4). Convert it to CMY and to HSV, showing each step of the arithmetic.
outline: Green is the maximum channel, so H = 60° × (2 + (B − R)/(max − min)) = 60° × (2 + 0.5) = 150°
State that H = 150° is a green-cyan hue

bank.q: Compare DDA and Bresenham's line algorithm for accuracy, speed and hardware suitability. Explain why integer-only arithmetic matters on a low-cost display controller.
outline: DDA: one division before the loop, then float additions; rounding error accumulates on long lines
Bresenham: integer additions and comparisons only, exact pixel choice, no drift
Bresenham needs no floating-point unit, so it suits cheap hardware
DDA generalises easily to any slope and to other curves
Both pick one pixel per step along the driving axis
Verdict: Bresenham is preferred in hardware and in most software rasterisers

bank.q: Explain the even-odd rule and the nonzero winding rule for deciding whether a pixel is inside a polygon. Show how a self-intersecting polygon is filled differently by the two rules.
outline: Even-odd: count crossings of a ray; odd = inside
Nonzero winding: add +1 or −1 per crossing depending on edge direction; nonzero = inside
Self-intersecting star shape: even-odd leaves the middle hole, nonzero fills it
Winding number formally = signed count of crossings
Practical effect: font outlines and overlapping paths behave differently
Choice depends on the intended artwork, not on correctness

bank.q: Trace the path of a single triangle from a model file to lit pixels on a monitor. Link output primitives, scan conversion, colour model and display hardware in one pipeline.
outline: Model gives three vertices in object coordinates
Transform to world, then camera, then clip space
Clipping removes parts outside the view volume
Rasteriser turns the triangle into fragments; scan-line or barycentric coverage decides which pixels are inside
Colour model: RGB values computed per vertex, interpolated across the triangle
Frame buffer stores the pixels; raster scan display refreshes them at the refresh rate
Aliasing appears at edges because coverage is sampled per pixel centre

bank.q: A photograph is sampled too coarsely and then displayed enlarged. Using sampling, quantisation and visual perception, explain the defects seen and how to reduce them.
outline: Sampling fixes pixel positions; too few samples lose detail and create aliasing
Quantisation to 8 bits per channel creates banding in smooth gradients
Enlarging shows block structure because new pixels are interpolated, not real data
Eye is sensitive to edges and contrast, so jagged and blocky edges are noticed first
Anti-aliasing by area averaging softens edges
Dithering trades spatial noise for reduced banding
Prevention: sample at least twice the highest scene frequency (Nyquist), store more bits per channel

glossary.def: One addressable colour cell of a raster grid.
The pixel dimensions of a display or image, written as width × height.
Pixels per inch — how densely pixels are packed when an image is displayed or printed.
Dots per inch — how many ink dots a printer lays down in one inch.
Width divided by height of a pixel or of the whole frame.
Bits stored per pixel; 24-bit colour uses 8 bits each for red, green and blue.
Memory area holding the colour of every pixel of the frame being displayed.
How many times per second the display redraws the picture, measured in hertz.
The set of line segments and commands a random scan display draws each refresh.
The software or hardware that turns shape descriptions into pixels.
The position of a colour on the colour wheel, measured as an angle from 0° to 360°.
How far a colour is from grey, from 0 (grey) to 1 (fully pure).
Brightness of a colour in HSV, equal to the largest of its R, G and B components.
A point with attributes such as position and colour, fed into the graphics pipeline.
A candidate pixel produced by rasterisation, before depth and blending tests.
A running quantity in a raster algorithm shown by its sign which pixel to choose next.
Line algorithm that steps along the longer axis by one unit and adds a fixed increment to the other axis.
Determining which pixels a shape covers and assigning them colour.
A contiguous run of pixels inside a polygon on a single scan line.
List of polygon edges bucketed by their smallest y value, used to start scan-line filling.
Edges crossing the current scan line, kept sorted by x so intersections come out in order.
Fill that spreads from a seed pixel until it meets pixels of a specified boundary colour.
Fill that spreads from a seed pixel to all connected neighbours sharing the seed's colour.
Signed count of how many times a polygon boundary wraps around a point; nonzero means inside under the nonzero rule.
Rounding a continuous value to the nearest of a finite set of levels.
Jagged edges or false patterns caused by sampling a continuous signal too coarsely.
